extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, constructive mathematicians, and graduate students studying foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and assess philosophical and mathematical arguments for constructive (intuitionistic/Bishop-style) mathematics, including their premises, consequences, and compatibility with mathematical practice. Emphasis on criteria such as meaning, computational content, relation to classical mathematics, and philosophical commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational role of the natural numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: “the primary concern of mathematics is number, and this means the positive integers” (Bishop). The development of the theory of the positive integers from the primitive concept of the unit, adjoining a unit, and induction carries complete conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the natural numbers as foundational for mathematics: prioritize formulations and interpretations that reduce to finitely performable operations on the integers. Connects to Kronecker and predicativism; justifies emphasis on finitary methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive interpretation of logical constants
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning of logical constants should be given in terms of available interpretations as finitely performable operations with the natural numbers; mathematical statements should have an interpretation that yields computational content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proofs/statements by whether their logical constants (¬, ∧, ∨, →, ∀, ∃) admit constructive readings tied to concrete finite procedures. Anti-pattern: accepting classical logical readings that lack finite computational interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-beings criterion (principle of 'in principle' performability)
rubrics_metrics.description: We are finite beings and should be concerned only with forms of mathematics that a finite being can carry out, at least in principle. 'In principle' allows infinite domains only insofar as finite methods interpret them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate methods by whether a finite agent could, in principle, carry out the required operations or whether the account presupposes non-finite powers (an 'infinite mind').

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness of classical quantification over infinite domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical quantification over infinite domains is questioned because its classical interpretation involves an infinite search through the domain; such quantification may lack descriptive meaning for finite man unless given an intuitionistic/constructive interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize universal/existential claims over infinite domains: require either constructive/intuitive procedures or justify why classical quantification is acceptable in context (e.g., finitary subcases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum non-finite ability: LPO as a yardstick
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop suggests that a minimum requirement for a being with non-finite powers is a form of limited omniscience, such as the principle LPO (ability to search a sequence of integers to determine whether they are all 0 or not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing powers to non-finite agents or adopting principles, check whether they amount to LPO-like capabilities. Use LPO as a diagnostic for how 'non-constructive' an assumption is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical meaningfulness determined by computational content
rubrics_metrics.description: For Bishop, mathematical meaning depends on the availability of computational (finitely performable) content; a proof of existence should show how to find the witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the acceptability of a theorem or proof partly by whether it yields explicit constructions/witnesses or computational procedures; non-constructive existence without such content is viewed as lacking meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform mathematics constructively rather than outright ban classical mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop advocates abandoning non-constructive proof methods to obtain computationally meaningful mathematics, but not necessarily declaring classical mathematics entirely illegitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor approaches that seek constructive reconstructions of classical results and treat classical proofs as a guide or challenge to find constructive analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional philosophical argument schema for intuitionistic logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional arguments typically move from philosophical considerations (nature of mathematical entities/our activity/language) to the conclusion that classical logic is illegitimate and should be replaced by intuitionistic logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating such arguments, identify the philosophical premises and check whether they entail the strong rejection of classical practice; note whether they overreach by declaring classical mathematics unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brouwerian argument for rejecting PEM in infinitary contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Math viewed as an essentially language-less mental activity; proofs are constructions. A purported proof of excluded middle would amount to a construction that either proves or reduces to absurdity any statement, which is implausible for infinite systems—PEM acceptable for finitary contexts only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this criterion by distinguishing finitary vs infinitary contexts: accept PEM for bounded/finitary cases but reject its blanket use over infinite domains absent constructive procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dummettian/semantic argument: use-determined meaning and verificationism
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning is communicable and observable; use exhaustively determines meaning. Classical logic embodies verification-transcendent truth and is thus rejected in favor of intuitionistic logic which aligns with verification-based meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess semantic/meaning-based defenses by asking whether the 'use' of language provides the required observables/verifications; scrutinize the move from semantic premises to rejecting classical truth notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection: anti-realism entanglement
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional arguments for intuitionistic logic are often tied to anti-realist positions (mind-dependence of mathematical entities or verificationist meaning), which many philosophers find unattractive or untenable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting or evaluating arguments, beware of implicit commitments to anti-realism; constructive mathematicians aiming for neutrality should avoid tying mathematics to strong anti-realist metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection: 'philosophy-first' worry
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue intuitionism exemplifies 'philosophy-first'—philosophical considerations dictate mathematical practice leading to revisionism; some defend anti-revisionism and resist philosophy imposing practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate philosophical premises that clarify meaning from speculative metaphysical claims; reasonable 'philosophy-first' moves should be those prompted by issues of meaning relevant to practice, not speculative ontology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic test for philosophy-first: mathematical fruitfulness matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an argument is philosophy-first, the constructive mathematician should ask whether the resulting mathematics is interesting and fruitful; banning philosophy-first a priori could obstruct development of useful mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate philosophical motivations by their mathematical consequences: if the methodology yields fertile new mathematics (e.g., intuitionistic logic led to new results), that counts in its favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too-strong objection: avoid outright rejection of classical mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional arguments are criticized as 'too strong' because they entail outright rejection or unintelligibility of classical mathematics; Bishop-style constructive mathematicians favor a more tolerant (liberal) stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer arguments that recommend constructive practice without declaring classical mathematics incoherent; check whether conclusions allow for classical methods as guides or parts playable within constructive analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal vs radical constructivism distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberal constructivist: constructive mathematics preferable but classical mathematics coherent/legitimate; Radical constructivist: classical mathematics is illegitimate and incoherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advocating constructivism, clarify whether one is taking a liberal (reconstructive/compatible) or radical (exclusionary) stance, and evaluate consequences for acceptance of classical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reverse mathematics as neutral analytic tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive reverse mathematics aims to clarify relations between concepts and theorems across mathematical practices and offers a 'neutral' perspective to analyze classical mathematics from a constructive standpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructive reverse mathematics to separate constructive cores from classical components and to analyze which principles are genuinely needed for classical theorems; treat it as a method to bridge practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three mathematical motivations for doing mathematics constructively
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) direct computational meaning (applicability to computers/pragmatic), (ii) greater generality (weaker theory -> more models -> more general theorems), (iii) refinement (availability of distinctions unavailable classically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending constructivism, foreground these mathematical advantages rather than solely philosophical premises. Use examples: algorithmic content, theorems valid in more models, and distinctions clarified by constructive analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against ontological reduction to natural numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Billinge suggests Bishop's assumptions might imply reducing all mathematics to natural numbers; the author argues Bishop does not commit to such ontological reduction but rather an epistemological emphasis on finite operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting constructive arguments as requiring ontological reduction of mathematical entities to naturals. Emphasize epistemological claims about methods and finitely performable operations instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological vs ontological constructivism distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Bridges' distinction: ontological constructivism (Brouwer—mathematical objects as mental creations) vs epistemological constructivism (Bishop—methodological focus motivating intuitionistic logic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing philosophical defenses, specify whether the claim is metaphysical (ontological) or methodological/epistemological; Bishop-style defenses should aim to be epistemological to avoid metaphysical commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for an acceptable philosophical defence of liberal constructivism
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate defence should justify constructivism without overreaching to radical constructivism, and should rely on mathematical advantages (computational content, generality, refinement) rather than speculative metaphysics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build arguments that show constructive methods yield tangible mathematical benefits and allow classical mathematics to coexist as guide/target for constructive reconstructions; avoid premises that force radical exclusion of classical practice.
